planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring into moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil under conifers or other acid-loving shrubs; Oregon wintergreen resents disturbance and establishes slowly.

directions: Oregon wintergreen is a low, mat-forming evergreen subshrub of moist coniferous forests and forest-edge seeps from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Coast Range to northern California and east to Idaho and Montana. It carries small, oval, leathery, glossy leaves on wiry trailing stems, with nodding white to pale pink urn-shaped flowers in early summer followed by round red berries that resemble a smaller version of its eastern relative, teaberry. Give it consistently moist, strongly acidic, well-drained duff or peaty soil in partial to full shade, ideally near established conifers or rhododendrons, and avoid lime, fertilizer, or heavy mulch turnover. It spreads slowly by rooting stems to form a modest evergreen carpet and is best treated as a patient, long-term planting rather than a quick-fill groundcover.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
E-Flora BC: Electronic Atlas of the Flora of British Columbia

planting.note: Move only nursery-propagated divisions with intact soil and root fungi attached, planted in spring directly into dry, acidic conifer duff; wild collection and standard garden soil both cause failure.

directions: Little Prince's Pine is a diminutive, semi-woody evergreen of dry pine and fir forests along the Pacific coast from British Columbia south through the Sierra Nevada and California Coast Ranges, usually found scattered singly or in loose colonies in deep needle duff. It is smaller and more delicate than its relative pipsissewa, with sparse whorls of narrow, sharply toothed, dark green leaves and one to a few nodding, waxy pink-and-white flowers held above the foliage in summer. Like other Chimaphila, it draws part of its nutrition from mycorrhizal fungi in the soil and is extremely difficult to establish outside of intact, undisturbed forest duff, so treat it as a specimen for admiring in situ rather than a reliable garden plant. Where nursery-propagated stock is available, tuck it into dry, lean, acidic soil beneath established pines with minimal root disturbance and no fertilizer or soil amendment, then leave it alone.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
Jepson eFlora, Jepson Flora Project, University of California, Berkeley

planting.note: Plant nursery divisions in spring into dry to lightly moist, acidic conifer duff with established mycorrhizal fungi; this species tolerates drier sites than most Pyrola but still resists transplanting.

directions: White-veined wintergreen grows in dry pine, fir, and mixed-conifer forests across the mountains of western North America from British Columbia to California and east into the Rockies, standing out among its relatives for the striking pale-white marbling along the veins of its dark green, leathery basal leaves. A slender flowering stalk rises in summer bearing a loose spike of nodding, waxy, greenish-white to purplish flowers with a distinctive curved style. Unlike many pyrolas that demand constant moisture, this species tolerates the drier duff of open pine forest, though it remains dependent on specific mycorrhizal fungi and is very slow to establish after transplant. Site it in undisturbed, acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade beneath conifers, avoid soil disturbance or fertilizer, and expect it to persist for years once settled rather than to spread quickly.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
E-Flora BC: Electronic Atlas of the Flora of British Columbia

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into acidic, humus-rich conifer or mixed-woodland soil with intact fungal associations; like other pyrolas it depends on mycorrhizal partners and resists cultivation in amended garden beds.

directions: Green-flowered wintergreen is a circumboreal woodland herb found across northern North America, Europe, and Asia in dry to moderately moist coniferous and mixed forests, often growing alongside other pyrolas but distinguished by its pale yellow-green, nodding, cup-shaped flowers held on a slender stalk above a low evergreen rosette of rounded leaves. It is one of the more cold-tolerant members of the genus, ranging well into boreal forest, but shares the family trait of depending on specific mycorrhizal fungi in undisturbed forest soil and transplants poorly once those associations are disturbed. Establish only nursery-propagated plants in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade near existing conifers, and leave the leaf litter layer intact to preserve the fungal network it relies on. Growth and spread are slow even under good conditions, so patience is essential.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
E-Flora BC: Electronic Atlas of the Flora of British Columbia
